overview: This card interprets the imported Swedes label as Svear and neighboring east-central Swedish communities from about 400 to 800 CE. It does not describe the modern Swedish nation, a continuous kingdom, or every inhabitant of present-day Sweden. Sparse outsider names, including sixth-century forms in Jordanes, cannot be matched automatically to archaeological objects or fixed territory. Evidence is strongest around Uppland and Lake Malaren: workshops at Helgo, monumental halls and mounds at Gamla Uppsala, boat graves at Valsgarde and Vendel, the Mojbro runic stone, and Birka's beginnings around 750. Farms, animals, food, craft, water, refuse, travel, care, and learning belonged to varied households as well as elite centers. Geats, Gotlanders, Sami, Finnic communities, and other neighbors remain distinct. The atlas underlines the danger of reading its outline literally. Its 400, 500, and 600 snapshots share a small Uppland-centered polygon; at 700 the same id suddenly stretches toward central Norway and overlaps a Sami layer. That is an editorial geometry change, not a surveyed expansion. At 800 the label disappears while people and institutions continue into a differently documented Viking-age landscape.

periods.title: 400 to 450: a regional opening, not a founding date
periods.summary: The map begins at 400, while Mojbro U 877 has a broad archaeological date of 375/400 to 560/570. Its Proto-Norse runes prove writing in Uppland, not a national foundation. Communities around Lake Malaren remain visible chiefly through settlements, graves, objects, and landscapes rather than self-authored political history.

periods.title: 450 to 500: specialized production at Helgo
periods.summary: Helgo's Migration-period workshops concentrated casting debris, raw metal, and unfinished work in an exceptional Lake Malaren setting. Isotope and trace-element analysis identifies both local lead and wider supply connections. Skilled production implies teaching and exchange, but it does not reveal a single ruler, ethnic workforce, or fixed market boundary.

periods.title: 500 to 550: outsider names enter the record
periods.summary: Jordanes listed many peoples of Scandza around the mid-sixth century, including names later connected with Svear. His compressed geography serves a Gothic history assembled far from Uppland. The catalogue is valuable textual evidence, but it cannot securely assign archaeological sites, household customs, or measured territory to each name.

periods.title: 550 to 600: Gamla Uppsala is monumentalized
periods.summary: Between roughly 550 and 650, builders reshaped Gamla Uppsala with great mounds, raised house platforms, halls, craft space, enclosures, hearth areas, roads, and paved yards. This concentrated labor and resources. Archaeology can demonstrate a powerful center without supplying a complete royal list or borders for its authority.

periods.title: 600 to 650: halls, workshops, and boat graves
periods.summary: The central complex at Gamla Uppsala and richly furnished boat graves at Valsgarde and Vendel show hierarchy, ceremony, skilled work, and extensive material connections. Most people were not buried this way. Exceptional graves disclose what mourners assembled for selected dead, not an inventory of every household or one standardized Svear society.

periods.title: 650 to 700: networks around elite landscapes
periods.summary: Valsgarde continued through boat inhumations and cremations, with objects, animals, and materials linking local burial choices to distant networks. Current research stresses that much of the complex record remains incompletely published. Richness supports elite display and connection, while the precise political organization behind each funeral remains open to study.

periods.title: 700 to 750: seafaring, kin, and violence
periods.summary: The Salme ship burials in Estonia date around 750. Isotopes and objects point many of the dead toward the Malaren region, while genomes identify close relatives. Their wounds show lethal conflict abroad. One extraordinary expedition reveals mobility and organized groups, but cannot define all Svear households or a national army.

periods.title: 750 to 800: Birka and a changing maritime world
periods.summary: Birka was founded around 750 on Bjorko and developed as a settlement and exchange center. Its Black Earth, defenses, graves, craft remains, and harbor landscape belong to the card's closing decades. The transition conventionally called Viking Age gathered pace without erasing older farms, centers, families, or regional differences.

sections.title: Exact identity, chronology, and atlas geometry

items.text: The exact id is swedes, indexed with that imported name from approximately 400 to 800. Coverage classifies it as a state, yet no exact card, card-index association, or researched override exists. This packet uses Svear and east-central Swedish communities, changes the kind to culture, and preserves the four-century interval.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The exact id appears once each in 400, 500, 600, and 700, matching coverage's four consecutive intervals. No feature lies outside the indexed lifetime, and no snapshot duplicates the target. The 300 file is empty at every tested regional probe.

The 400, 500, and 600 files reuse one Polygon: one component, one ring, 51 positions, and a box from about 15.29 to 19.04 east and 58.64 to 60.31 north. Its centroid near 17.07 east, 59.61 north describes the drawing, not a capital or population center.

The 700 polygon has 209 positions and grows nearly twelvefold in planar exterior area, reaching about 4.98 east, 64.10 north, and central Norway. Gamla Uppsala remains inside, but Birka, Helgo, and Stockholm remain outside. This cartographic enthusiasm is not evidence of a sudden Scandinavian annexation.

At 700 the target shares topology arcs with danes, saami, west-getaes, and east-getaes, and its area overlaps the saami feature. At 800 it vanishes; Uppsala probes become swedes-and-goths while Trondheim becomes northmen. These are atlas layers, so successors and predecessors stay empty and the separate later card remains separate.

Jordanes wrote Getica around 551 as a history of the Goths and compressed many Scandza peoples into a short catalogue. Suehans and Suetidi are often connected with later Svear traditions, but his spelling and geography do not provide a census, native self-description, or dependable border map for sixth-century Sweden.

Archaeological scholarship locates historical Sviars or Svear chiefly in the Malaren region of east-central Sweden, especially around Uppland. That regional frame is useful, but it remains an interpretation joining later names with material evidence. A burial custom or brooch style cannot independently announce its owner's ethnic identity.

Isotopes from the Salme dead point many individuals toward east-central Sweden, while several could fit Gotland or other places. Childhood tooth enamel records geological exposure rather than a passport. Objects, burial treatment, and isotope baselines make a Malaren origin plausible, but each method retains geographic and biographical uncertainty.

Large-scale ancient DNA shows Scandinavian populations were regionally structured and also connected beyond Scandinavia. At Salme, close biological kin travelled together, yet genomes do not name a language, legal status, or ethnic affiliation. Genetic similarity can test relationships and ancestry; it cannot certify that every sampled person called himself a Svear.

Sandby Borg on Oland preserves twenty-six unburied people killed between about 400 and 550. It is powerful evidence for violence within present-day Sweden, but Oland is outside this card's core and the atlas leaves Gotland and other communities distinct. Modern geography alone must not turn every contemporary site into Svear evidence.

Gamla Uppsala's 550 to 650 complex joined great mounds with raised platforms, a roughly 50-meter hall, craft buildings, hearth zones, fences, paved yards, and roads. These features required planned labor and repeated rebuilding. They show a magnate center embedded in a larger settlement, not a freestanding palace with known administrative departments.

Research combines new excavation, survey, GIS, and reassessment of older trenches to place Gamla Uppsala's monuments within an estate. Workshops, economy buildings, resource use, fences, and processional-looking post rows formed a connected landscape. Individual features once studied alone make more sense together, although their precise ceremonies and governance remain debated.

At Helgo, workshop activity changed around the 530s, cemeteries began, and evidence suggests more permanent habitation. Ritual activity may have shifted from an outdoor offering place into a hall. Linking every change directly to the 536 atmospheric event is an interpretation; contemporaneity alone does not prove one household-level response.

Settlement and agriculture around Old Uppsala developed through many farms as well as the central estate. Livestock, fields, consumption, and surplus tied ordinary production to concentrated demand. Archaeology can compare scales of buildings and food supply, but a modest outbuilding does not identify a servant, tenant, enslaved worker, or owner by itself.

Birka began around 750, late in this card, with a defended settlement area later called the Black Earth and extensive cemeteries. Only part has been excavated. Estimates of 500 to 1,000 inhabitants describe its developed Viking-age phase, so they should not be projected unchanged onto its first decades.

sections.title: Food, farming, animals, and daily work

items.text: Farms around Gamla Uppsala combined crop cultivation and livestock management while supplying their own households and, at times, central consumption. Seasonal work included preparing soil, tending animals, harvesting, processing grain, storing food, and maintaining buildings. The evidence supports coordinated labor without assigning every recurring task permanently by sex or rank.

Archaeobotanical investigations at Vendel and Valsgarde compare plant remains from settlements and graves. Grain, food residues, and grave deposits require different interpretations: a seed in a hearth may reflect cooking or accident, while food placed with the dead records funeral choice. Neither context alone reconstructs a universal daily menu.

Nitrogen isotopes in charred cereals can detect long-term manuring practices. Samples from southern Swedish Migration and Vendel contexts show cultivation varied through time and between sites. Manure could sustain soil fertility and yields, but the study does not make one field system representative of Uppland or every household in the atlas polygon.

Valsgarde boat graves contained animals and everyday equipment alongside conspicuous weapons and dress. Researchers now study animal offerings rather than treating them as scenery for elite objects. Dogs, horses, cattle, and birds can reveal husbandry and ritual selection, while grave abundance cannot be converted directly into the deceased person's ordinary diet.

At Helgo, bread appeared regularly in graves after the mid-sixth-century changes described by excavators. A loaf placed for burial reflects production skills and ritual choice at once. It confirms cereal food without revealing the full recipe, who baked it, how often living households ate similar bread, or whether everyone shared access.

Genome analysis at Salme identifies four brothers buried near one another and additional close kin among men who died together. Family ties could therefore structure at least one travelling group. The sample is male, violent, and exceptional, so it cannot define marriage rules, residence patterns, or everyday family composition back in Malaren settlements.

The Salme bodies were carefully recorded in stacked burial layers after lethal conflict. Their arrangement combined practical handling with deliberate treatment. Biological kin, companions, leaders, and dependents may all have travelled together, but shared burial does not make every person a relative, nor does weapon equipment reveal each man's household position.

Children entered social worlds through play, imitation, work, and staged expectations. Some Scandinavian graves include gaming pieces or full-sized martial equipment with young people, but funeral objects express adult choices as well as a child's life. They cannot show that every child trained for war or wanted the role mourners displayed.

Boat graves at Valsgarde and nearby sites highlight a narrow, privileged selection from a much larger population. Cremations and less furnished graves represent other commemorative choices. Wealthy funerals reveal gatherings, obligations, skilled preparation, and social competition, yet they leave ordinary partnerships, adoption, fosterage, and household dependency far less visible.

The great hall and adjacent work areas at Gamla Uppsala brought hosts, craftspeople, laborers, visitors, and dependents into shared space. Architecture can indicate scale and access, but not a complete seating plan or household roster. Social rank likely shaped experience, while individual relationships must be inferred from several kinds of evidence.

No source documents a standardized school, enrollment age, classroom, or curriculum for these communities between 400 and 800. Children nevertheless had to learn speech, seasonal routines, animal handling, food preparation, navigation, etiquette, stories, and craft. Archaeology makes skill transmission necessary while rarely preserving who taught whom or at what age.

The Old Uppsala workshop contained a drawplate used to pull silver through successively smaller holes. Producing reliable wire required material judgment, controlled force, maintenance, and repeated practice. Such a tool implies trained knowledge, probably learned through demonstration and correction, although it does not identify an apprentice, workshop school, or written manual.

Helgo metalworkers handled brass, copper, lead, ingots, rods, casting waste, molds, and finished forms. Provenance analysis shows local and long-distance supply. Learning therefore included recognizing materials and managing heat as well as shaping objects. The debris records production decisions, but it cannot recover every spoken instruction or name the craft community's language.

Mojbro U 877 demonstrates that someone in Uppland knew the older runic system during this card's opening centuries. Its short inscription is not evidence for broad literacy, public schooling, or an official Svear chancery. Rune knowledge could circulate through restricted personal teaching, and the surviving stone represents only one durable use of it.

Games in high-status burials may reflect leisure, strategic display, social training, or funeral symbolism. Child-focused archaeology warns that miniature and adult-sized objects do not have one automatic meaning. A gaming set can suggest learned rules and companions, but it does not preserve the rules sheet, lesson plan, or the loser's excuses.

Dental study of an agricultural Swedish Early Iron Age population records caries and other oral conditions through direct examination of teeth. Such lesions connect diet, bacteria, age, wear, and care in complicated ways. The cemetery lies outside the Svear core, so it offers comparison rather than a disease rate for this card.

At Sandby Borg, skeletons preserve perimortem violence and a demographic cross-section of people left unburied after an attack. Trauma can identify weapons and circumstances more securely than motives. The site shows what conflict could do to bodies, but its island community and catastrophic event cannot stand for ordinary health across east-central Sweden.

The Salme dead carried many sharp-force injuries, providing direct evidence of lethal combat around 750. Isotope work samples tooth enamel formed in childhood, which survives differently from injured adult bone. Together these methods reconstruct origin and death, but reveal much less about earlier illness, wound care, pain, disability, or recovery.

Valsgarde's unburned boat graves preserve selected bodies and objects, while many surrounding cremations transform bone and reduce diagnostic detail. Modern imaging and chemical analysis can recover hidden construction and material information without dismantling corroded finds. These methods improve evidence but do not turn grave equipment into prescriptions or identify a healer.

No consulted source preserves a medical handbook, named practitioner, dosage, surgical instruction, or standardized treatment attributable to Svear communities from 400 to 800. People surely nursed illness and injury, but bones mainly record stress, disease, trauma, and survival. Remedies, symptoms, bedside decisions, and emotional care usually remain unrecorded.

Birka occupied Bjorko in Lake Malaren, so boats, shoreline access, and freshwater surroundings structured the settlement. Offshore sediments preserve a distinct layer produced by town activity. Water carried people and goods, but it also received material removed from houses, ditches, storage areas, livestock spaces, and latrines.

Researchers interpret Birka's offshore layer as including latrine cleanings, cut shoreline plants, ditch and storage cleaning, domestic-animal dung, and deposits made on winter ice. This is direct sanitation evidence from the card's final decades. It records repeated removal and dumping rather than a sewer network or universal household toilet.

Geophysical survey and excavation identified a lost moat along part of Birka's boundary. A moat could shape drainage, movement, and defense, but its discovery does not make it a clean-water supply or municipal sewer. Less than a tenth of the Black Earth has been excavated, leaving many household arrangements unresolved.

Rural farms around Gamla Uppsala depended on local wells, streams, precipitation, drainage, and labor, although the broad agrarian synthesis does not establish one water design for every farm. Animal dung could fertilize fields while poorly placed waste contaminated living areas. Daily sanitation was a household practice before it was infrastructure.

The evidence supports latrine cleaning at early Birka, but not standardized toilets, piped water, sewers, or municipal refuse collection across all Svear communities. Elsewhere, pits, hearth cleaning, animal management, dumping, and drainage must be described site by site. No eighth-century plumbing inspector left a conveniently complete report.

sections.title: Craft, exchange, and the Mojbro inscription

items.text: The Old Uppsala drawplate retains silver residue in its holes, supporting its identification as a wire-making tool from the sixth- to eighth-century fine-metal workshop beside the hall. Thin wire served complex ornament production. The object links technical achievement with elite demand without proving that rulers personally directed each craft decision.

At Helgo, lead isotope and trace-element analysis found Swedish lead among a wider collection of imported or uncertain metals. Ingots, rods, and waste show supply before finished display. Exchange connected local craft to distant sources, but an object's raw material route need not equal its maker's birthplace or political allegiance.

Helgo's accumulated molds and crucibles attest intensive casting before activity changed in the sixth century. Later evidence includes advanced metalworking in a reorganized settlement. Production centers could rise, contract, and repurpose without their communities simply vanishing. Workshops were dynamic institutions, even when archaeology preserves more broken equipment than staff meetings.

Secure written-language sample: Mojbro U 877, found at Mojbro in Hagby parish, Uppland, dated 375/400 to 560/570. Script: Elder Futhark, called Proto-Norse in the database. Normalized Unicode rune display: ᚠᚱᚨᚹᚨᚱᚨᛞᚨᛉ ᚨᚾᚨᚺᚨᚺᚨ ᛁᛊ ᛊᛚᚨᚷᛁᚾᚨᛉ. Transliteration: “frawaradaz anahaha is| |slaginaz.”

The database's Proto-Norse normalization is “Frawaradaz <anahaha> is slaginaz.” Its English translation is “Frawaradaz <anahaha> is killed.” The uncertain element stays bracketed. Carver and author are unknown. Attribution: inscription U 877, Scandinavian Runic-text Database, Uppsala University, served by the Swedish National Heritage Board; object SHM 24203.

Valsgarde's fifteen unlooted boat graves include rare helmets, glass, weapons, tools, and carefully documented rivets. Their achievement is both ancient and archaeological: complex funerals survived, and excavators recorded fragile relationships among objects. Spectacular preservation should not obscure the cremations, chamber graves, settlement, and many people outside elite burial.

For more than four centuries, prominent people of both sexes were buried at Valsgarde in boats, chambers, and cremations with objects and animals. Eastern connections reached far beyond the Baltic, though their routes and meanings remain under study. Long-distance contact was an enduring capacity, not proof of control over every connected place.

Cereal isotope evidence shows farmers actively managed soil fertility in first-millennium Sweden. That quiet achievement underwrote households, feasts, animals, workshops, and monumental labor. Agricultural knowledge varied by field and period, so the result is more useful as evidence of skilled adaptation than as a claim that one authority dictated identical farming practice.

Birka's founding around 750 added a durable exchange and craft settlement to the Malaren landscape. The Black Earth, graves, rampart, and later harbor works record concentrated activity and wide connections. Birka was not the inevitable capital of a timeless Sweden; its early growth belonged to a changing regional political economy.

The rediscovered Birka moat changes interpretation of part of the town boundary and shows how even famous sites remain incomplete. Defensive works, halls, mounds, craft centers, seafaring groups, and runic knowledge were major achievements of the period. None alone supplies the constitution, borders, or continuous dynasty of a unified Swedes state.

ending.text: Around 800, the communities described here did not disappear. Farms, families, craft knowledge, ritual landscapes, and maritime routes continued. Gamla Uppsala's sixth- to eighth-century estate changed during the eighth or ninth century, and Valsgarde remained in use. The atlas performs a sharper edit: swedes is removed, the Uppsala probes receive swedes-and-goths, Trondheim receives northmen and later norway, and Helsinki receives finns before another repaint. Those labels do not document one succession ceremony. The immense 700 polygon overlaps saami and had already exceeded the earlier Uppland footprint, so treating its removal as a kingdom's fall would compound the geometry error. This card ends as a transformation with no asserted predecessor or successor. The separately indexed swedes-and-goths record remains separate, and medieval Sweden requires its own evidence rather than automatic inheritance from every earlier person, place, or name.
